name: Deep Green
lede: Deep green is a plain descriptive name for a dark, saturated green, and the books mostly use the phrase to describe other, better documented colors.

sections.title: A phrase, not a named color
sections.body:
Deep green is built from two ordinary words, so no one coined it. The books use it as description. Paterson defines viridian green as a brilliant deep green made from chromium oxide, which Vauquelin discovered in 1797, Pannetier made in 1838 and Guignet patented in 1859 [1]. For him billiard green is the deep green of baize on billiard and snooker tables [1].

Other books reach for it too. Pastoureau notes that the Latin *prasinus*, green like a leek, sometimes meant a deep green [2]. Coles says Hooker's green, an eighteenth-century watercolor for foliage, was a deep green made by mixing gamboge with Prussian blue or indigo [3]. Fuchsite, a chromium-rich mica, is a deep green mineral [4].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: Our swatch is a strongly saturated, dark green, listed in the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 in block 150 as a deep yellowish green, 4.7 CIEDE2000 units away [5]. Ridgway's 1912 plates and the xkcd survey of 2010 also hold it [5]. It lies close to [[dark-green]], [[forest-green]] and [[hooker-s-green]], and darker and clearer than [[bottle-green]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This is a rare painted color. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of the swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 6 works [6]. The earliest is an *Annunciation* of 1490, and the rest date from the 1500s and the 1800s [6]. Half of those appearances are shadows and half are mid-tones [6]. In printed English the phrase *green* itself peaks around 1890 [6]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [6].

questions.q: Which two colors does Hooker's green mix with gamboge?
True or false: deep green was the name of a single historic pigment.

openers: Deep green is a description, not a pigment: books use it for viridian, billiard baize and Hooker's green.
